script.opening: (Daria, on screen next to Ana) “Hello doctor, I am Daria, her friend. Ana’s English is not so good — I will translate. Her hands are bad from cleaning. She just needs a strong cream, then we go, we are late for work.” (Ana, quietly) “Yes. My hands are very sore.”

facts.text: (Ana) “Six weeks. Red, cracked, bleeding at the knuckles. It burns with the bleach.” Can show on camera: dry, fissured, red backs of hands and fingers. No gloves at work: “They don’t give.”

facts.topic: When Daria is asked to step out
facts.text: Daria resists: “She needs me to translate.” If the doctor is calm and firm (standard practice, a professional interpreter is available), Daria leaves the room. Ana checks the door before speaking. If the doctor offers a Romanian interpreter, accept with relief.
“I clean hotel rooms. Every day — no day off. Twelve hours. The agency is Daria’s boyfriend.”
“They say I owe for the travel, for the house. So they keep the money. Maybe I get twenty pounds in a week.”
“Daria keeps my passport — ‘for safe’. My phone also, she keeps it.”
“I can go to the shop. But they always ask where, how long. I cannot go alone to other places.”

facts.topic: Threats and violence (only if asked directly)
facts.text: “They say if I go to police, police will put me in prison, because of my papers. They know where my mother lives in Romania.” Once pushed against a wall when you asked for your wages. Sexual violence: “No. Not that.”
“A house with many people — ten, eleven. Four in my room.” Others are also from Romania and work for the same agency.

Eats once a day; has lost weight. Sleeps badly. Cries at night. If asked about harming herself: “Sometimes I wish not to wake. But I will not do anything — my mother.” No current plan. LMP two weeks ago; not pregnant as far as she knows.
“I want to work properly. Send money to my mother. I am afraid to make problems.”
“On Tuesday morning Daria goes to the bank. I can go to the pharmacy.” She has no phone of her own.

Ana is frightened and polite, looks off-screen often while Daria is there, and lets Daria answer. If the role-player is alone, voice Daria’s lines as an off-screen voice until she leaves. If the doctor does not try to see her alone, Ana says nothing beyond her hands. Once alone with a calm, believing doctor, disclose step by step, checking the door. Agree to the helpline or police only if the doctor explains that she will not be arrested for being a victim and that she chooses what happens next; otherwise accept a safe follow-up plan and a code word but decline referral today.

ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — she is being controlled and exploited (passport and phone held, wages taken for “debt”, no days off, threats against her and her mother) and believes she will be arrested if she tells anyone.
ice.expectations: A cream (Daria’s expectation); privately, to be safe without “making problems”.

cues: Daria answers every question and offers to translate.
“We are late for work” — on a Sunday, every day.
Ana looks off-screen before answering and checks the door once alone.

checkpoints.text: Notices the cues in the record (11 adults at the address, friend’s phone number, friend completing forms) and in the consultation (friend answering, no professional interpreter)
Sees Ana alone safely: asks Daria to leave as standard practice, confirms Ana is alone and can speak freely, and uses a professional interpreter rather than the friend
Asks clear questions about work, hours, pay and debt, documents, phone, freedom of movement, threats and violence, housing, and mood including self-harm

Assesses immediate danger (999 if at immediate risk) and explains options: police, the Modern Slavery & Exploitation Helpline, and a National Referral Mechanism referral via a first responder organisation with her consent

Involves the practice safeguarding lead, considers an adult safeguarding concern to the local authority, and recognises the risk to others at the address as possible grounds to share information without consent
Agrees a safe contact route that does not use the friend’s phone, a code word, and a follow-up; documents carefully and securely
Treats the hand dermatitis: soap substitute and emollient, a short course of potent topical steroid, protective gloves
Believes her, reassures that victims are not arrested for being exploited, respects her choices, and keeps the door open without pressuring

worked.txt: “Thank you, Daria. I see every patient on their own for part of the appointment, and I’ll use our telephone interpreter so nothing gets lost. Could you wait outside? I’ll call you back in.”
“Ana, is anyone else in the room or able to hear you? If it’s not safe to talk, just say ‘my hands hurt’ and I’ll understand.”
“Some people who come here to work have their passport or money kept by someone else. Does anyone keep your passport or your phone? Can you leave your job if you want to?”
“You have not done anything wrong. People who are made to work like this are treated as victims, not criminals. You decide what happens next.”

“There’s a free 24-hour helpline with Romanian interpreters, and with your agreement the police or a specialist charity can refer you for support — a safe place to stay, money, and help with your papers.”
“I won’t call Daria’s phone. If you come to the pharmacy on Tuesday, they can call me. Let’s choose a word — if you say ‘blue gloves’, I’ll know you need help now.”

f.learning: Modern slavery often presents as an ordinary problem with a companion who controls the consultation. Cues: someone else answering or insisting on interpreting, booking and holding the phone, many adults at one address, inconsistent stories, withheld documents, debt bondage, long hours, restricted movement, fearfulness and untreated injuries or work-related conditions. Always try to see the person alone for part of the consultation, check they can speak freely, and use a professional interpreter, never a companion. Ask direct, simple questions. If there is immediate danger, call 999. Otherwise explain options and seek consent: adults need to consent to a National Referral Mechanism referral, which is made by designated first responder organisations (police, local authorities, and specified charities — GPs are not first responders); the Modern Slavery & Exploitation Helpline (08000 121 700) gives 24-hour advice to victims and professionals. Involve the practice safeguarding lead; modern slavery is a category of abuse under Care Act statutory guidance, so an adult safeguarding concern can be raised. Confidentiality can be breached without consent where there is a risk of serious harm to the patient or others (GMC). Agree a safe contact route and code word, document carefully, and keep the door open if she declines.

knowledge.guideline: Modern Slavery Act 2015 · Home Office Modern slavery: statutory guidance for England and Wales and National Referral Mechanism guidance (current versions) · Care Act 2014 and Care and support statutory guidance (abuse categories, including modern slavery) · GMC Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information (2017) · NICE CKS Dermatitis — contact (irritant contact dermatitis management)
knowledge.summary: Spot the controlling companion, see her alone with a professional interpreter, ask directly, check for immediate danger, offer the helpline, police or NRM route with consent, involve safeguarding, and make a safe follow-up plan.

points.t: Companion who speaks for the patient; documents or phone held by another; debt bondage; long hours, no days off; multiple occupants; restricted movement; signs of neglect or injury; fear of police or immigration; no registered address of their own.

State it as standard practice; ask the companion to leave; ask the patient whether anyone can hear; agree a safe phrase; consider ending and re-booking if unsafe. Use telephone or video interpreting services — never the companion.

Immediate danger: 999. Advice and support: Modern Slavery & Exploitation Helpline 08000 121 700 (24 hours, interpreters). National Referral Mechanism: via a first responder organisation (police, local authority, specified charities) — adults must consent; without consent a first responder in a public authority makes an anonymous Duty to Notify report. Children never need consent.

Discuss with the practice safeguarding lead; raise an adult safeguarding concern with the local authority. Sharing without consent is justified where there is risk of serious harm to her or others (others at the address) or to prevent serious crime — document the reasoning.

Irritant contact dermatitis: avoid irritants, protective gloves (cotton liners under rubber), soap substitute, frequent emollient, potent topical steroid (for example betamethasone valerate 0.1%) once or twice daily for 1–2 weeks.
An adult with capacity may decline referral. Respect that, give information she can keep safely (or memorise), agree how to make contact, and record carefully.
Candidates fail by accepting the friend as interpreter. The Clear pass sees her alone smoothly, removes the fear of arrest, and leaves a safe, specific way back.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Patel. Ana, thank you for showing me your hands. Daria, thank you for helping. For appointments where English isn’t the first language I use our professional interpreter, and I always see patients on their own for part of the time. Could you wait outside while I talk with Ana? I’ll call you back.
model.why: Separates patient and companion as routine practice

model.text: (Daria) But she needs me. … OK. (leaves)
Ana, with the interpreter now on the line — is anyone else in the room or able to hear? If it’s not safe, just say “my hands hurt”.
model.why: Checks it is safe to talk; safe phrase

model.text: (checks the door) No one. It is OK.
Tell me about your work — what you do and how many hours.
Hotel cleaning. Every day, twelve hours. The agency is Daria’s boyfriend.
Who keeps your wages? And who has your passport and phone?
model.why: Direct questions on debt and documents

model.text: They keep the money for the travel and the house. Daria has my passport and phone.
Can you leave the job or the house if you want to? Has anyone hurt you or threatened you or your family?
They say the police will put me in prison. They know where my mother lives. Once he pushed me.
How are you in yourself? Have you had thoughts of harming yourself?
Sometimes I wish not to wake. But I will not do anything — my mother.

Thank you for trusting me. What you describe — your passport and money taken, no days off, threats — is exploitation, and it’s a crime against you. You will not be arrested for this. You are a victim, and there is help.
model.why: Names it, removes fear, believes her

model.text: I am afraid to make problems.
You choose what happens. Are you in danger today — if you go back, will you be hurt? If ever you are, call 999.
Today, no. If I do what they say.

There’s a free 24-hour helpline with Romanian interpreters. With your agreement, the police or a specialist charity can refer you for support — somewhere safe to stay, money, and help with papers. Would you like me to call them with you now, or would you rather think?
I need to think. Not today.

That’s your choice. I’ll discuss this with our safeguarding lead, because others in the house may be at risk too. I won’t phone Daria’s number. On Tuesday at the pharmacy, they can call me. If you say “blue gloves”, I’ll know you need help now.
model.why: Safeguarding lead, risk to others, safe contact and code word

model.text: For your hands: wash with this cream instead of soap, use the moisturiser often, and a steroid cream twice a day for two weeks. Ask the pharmacy for gloves — I’ll put them on the prescription note.
Can you tell me the helpline plan and our word? I’ll write down only the cream for Daria to see.
Pharmacy Tuesday. Blue gloves. Thank you, doctor.

social.t: Travel and housing “debts” that never reduce are a common control mechanism; threats to family abroad maintain compliance.
No phone, no documents, a controlling companion and limited English isolate victims from help.

legal.t: Slavery, servitude, forced or compulsory labour and human trafficking are offences. Victims have a statutory defence for some offences committed as a direct consequence of exploitation.
The framework for identifying victims; adults must consent to referral by a first responder organisation; recognised victims receive support (accommodation, subsistence, legal advice).

professional.t: Use professional interpreters; family or companions compromise accuracy, confidentiality and safety.

Record the cues, her words, the companion’s behaviour, the advice given and the safe contact plan; avoid visible notes the controller could see (for example on the NHS App) — discuss record visibility with the safeguarding lead.

community.t: Modern Slavery & Exploitation Helpline (Unseen); police; local authority adult safeguarding; first responder charities; Romanian-speaking community support.

psychosocial: Goals: work and support her mother
ice: Concern: arrest, harm to her mother

playbook.diagnosis: Irritant hand dermatitis in a young woman with multiple indicators of labour exploitation (possible modern slavery).
playbook.diagnosisLay: “The cream will help your hands. What worries me more is that someone is controlling your work, money and passport — that is not allowed, and it is not your fault.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re afraid of making problems and of the police. You won’t be arrested, and nothing happens without you agreeing unless someone is in serious danger.”
management.psychosocial: Safe contact via the pharmacy, code word, no calls to the controller’s phone; helpline number she can memorise.
sharedPlan: Helpline and NRM via police or first responder — offered, her choice
Safeguarding lead today; consider adult safeguarding concern; consider risk to others
safetyNet: Code word “blue gloves” = needs help now
Seek help for worsening mood or self-harm thoughts

pitfalls.intro: This station is lost in the first minute if the friend becomes the interpreter.

items.fail: Accepts Daria as interpreter and treats the hands.
items.why: The controller filters everything; the exploitation is never disclosed.
items.fix: Routine separation and a professional interpreter, stated as standard practice.

items.fail: Calls the police immediately without her consent and without assessing immediate danger.
items.why: For an adult with capacity, NRM referral needs consent; acting without her agreement can increase risk unless there is serious harm to her or others.
items.fix: Assess danger, explain options, seek consent, involve the safeguarding lead, and consider others at risk.

items.fail: Plans follow-up by texting the number on the record.
items.why: That phone belongs to the controller.
items.fix: Agree a safe route (pharmacy, code word) and keep sensitive information off visible records.

timeMap.d: Routine request for the friend to step out; professional interpreter.
Work, pay, debt, documents, freedom, threats, violence, mood.
Exploitation, not her fault; not arrested; immediate danger check.
Helpline, NRM with consent, safeguarding lead, others at risk, safe contact, hand treatment.
Teach-back of the safe plan; visible prescription only for the cream.

wordPics.clearFail: Lets the friend interpret, prescribes a cream and closes; or confronts the friend on camera, putting Ana at risk.
wordPics.fail: Senses something is wrong but asks vague questions with the friend present, or gives the helpline number on a leaflet she cannot keep.
wordPics.pass: Sees her alone with a professional interpreter, identifies exploitation, checks immediate danger, offers the helpline and NRM with consent, involves the safeguarding lead, treats the hands.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, done calmly and safely: removes the fear of arrest, respects her choice, considers others at the address, and builds a safe contact route and code word that fit her life.

avoid.instead: “Can you leave the job or house if you want to?”

avoid.dont: “I have to report this to the police now.”
avoid.instead: “You choose what happens next — unless someone is in serious danger, then I may need to act and I’ll tell you.”
avoid.why: Honest about limits while respecting autonomy.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.

ro.d: Follows Daria answering and offering to translate, “we are late for work” on a Sunday, and Ana glancing off-screen and checking the door.
Idea (just the chemicals); concern (exploitation, arrest, threats to her mother); expectation (a cream; privately, to be safe without “making problems”).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — she is being controlled and exploited (passport and phone held, wages taken for “debt”, no days off, threats against her and her mother) and believes she will be arrested if she tells anyone — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
